title: Father Calls Co-Pilot Daughter Killed in Florida Learjet Crash 'a Hero'
excerpt: Allan Filgueiras says he has replayed 20-year-old Nathalia's final radio calls repeatedly, as NTSB investigators examine tail pieces found miles from the Greenacres crash site that killed nine.
body:
• Allan Filgueiras, himself a pilot, spoke publicly on Friday for the first time since his 20-year-old daughter Nathalia, the co-pilot of a Learjet 60, died with eight others in the November 1 crash near Greenacres, Florida.
  • He said he has replayed her final air traffic control calls repeatedly, and praised her composure: "She made me so proud. She showed me what it is to be a hero."
  • The National Transportation Safety Board says investigators have recovered part of an engine and three pieces of the jet's left elevator up to 3.8 miles from the crash site, evidence they are examining to determine whether parts of the aircraft separated before impact.
  • The family, represented by attorney Stuart Grossman, says no lawsuit has been filed and pushed back against online speculation about the co-pilot's age, noting she held a pilot's licence at 17 and had logged more than 1,300 flight hours.

Nearly a week after a Learjet 60 crashed near Greenacres in Palm Beach County, killing all nine people on board, the father of the jet's 20-year-old co-pilot spoke publicly for the first time on Friday, remembering his daughter as a gifted pilot who fought to control the aircraft until the final minute.

Allan Filgueiras appeared alongside attorney Stuart Grossman at a news conference in Coral Gables, according to the Palm Beach Post and Fox 13 News. Filgueiras, a pilot who taught his daughter to fly, said he has listened to her final air traffic control transmissions over and over, searching for a clue to what happened.

"She made me so proud. She showed me what it is to be a hero because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys, military or whatever, they can't handle it. And she was the one over there fighting to the last minute."

— Allan Filgueiras, father of co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras

Her final minutes in the cockpit

Nathalia Filgueiras, of Boca Raton, was the second-in-command on the private jet, which was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed around 1 p.m. on Sunday, November 1, near a mobile home park community. Hers was the voice on the air traffic control recording describing the problems the aircraft was having in its final minutes.

She reported calmly that the jet was accumulating ice on its wings and experiencing turbulence, then declared an emergency as it began descending rapidly. In the recording, reported by the Palm Beach Post, she is heard saying the aircraft was descending at more than 20,000 feet per minute and banking steeply, before her final words: "We're gonna crash! ... we're out of time!"

"I wanted to be by her side," her father said, his voice breaking, "to help." He described her as his "soulmate," and recalled that she could hardly believe she was paid to do what she loved most: "She used to say, 'Dad, can you believe that I would pay for this, but they actually pay me?'"

What investigators have found

The National Transportation Safety Board said on November 5 that excavation of the crash site was continuing and that investigators had recovered part of one of the jet's engines. Debris was recovered around the crater left by the impact along Military Road, including pieces found on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings.

Investigators also found three pieces of the Learjet's left elevator between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from where the aircraft crashed, according to the NTSB briefing reported by the Palm Beach Post. The elevator is a movable section on the tail that helps control the aircraft's pitch, and the pieces accounted for most of the tail — evidence investigators are examining to determine whether parts of the aircraft separated before impact. The aircraft nose-dived into the ground at an almost 90-degree vertical angle.

The jet was crossing Palm Beach County at about 12:50 p.m. when the crew reported icing, moderate turbulence and altitude deviations of 700 feet, the Post reported. Flying above 35,000 feet, the crew asked to climb higher; seconds later, Filgueiras reported the aircraft was descending and declared an emergency. Severe thunderstorms in the area created dangerous icing and turbulence conditions that investigators are examining. No cause has been determined.

The nine people who died

The crash killed Filgueiras, pilot Jeff Gregory, 55, and seven passengers: Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their two children Emma and Charlie, the family's nanny Anita Maria Ramírez Cetina, and Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, friends of the family travelling with them.

A defence of her record

Grossman pushed back against online speculation that Filgueiras was too young or inexperienced to serve as co-pilot. She earned her private pilot's licence at 17, before she had a driver's licence, and had logged more than 1,300 flight hours before November 1. "Nathalia was beyond an average pilot, she was extraordinary," Grossman said. "She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years."

She had first asked her father to teach her to fly at 12; their favourite outing was flying to Key West for coffee, then crossing South Florida to Naples for another cup the same day. In later years the roles reversed: "When we flew together, I used to instruct her. But then she became my instructor," he said. Chris Kirk, one of her first instructors, called her a "naturally gifted pilot" in a Facebook post: "That young lady was born to fly." Teachers at West Boca Raton Community High School, which she attended, also rejected criticism of her age.

Grossman said the family is not suing anyone at this time and will wait for government investigators to complete their work. "It's like ripping my heart out of my chest," Allan Filgueiras said. "Nathalia doesn't want to see a father falling apart, so I have to find a way to make her proud."
